notes.summary: An analogy gives you one pair with a hidden relationship and asks for another pair with the same relationship. The pair can be words (Doctor : Hospital), letters (ACE : BDF), numbers (4 : 16) or figures. SSC asks 2 to 3 analogy questions in Tier 1 and some in Tier 2. Number-based analogies are the most common, then word and letter types.

concepts.title: How to read an analogy
concepts.body:
A : B :: C : D is read as "A is to B as C is to D". The relation that takes A to B must also take C to D.
  • "Select the option related to the third word in the same way as the second is related to the first" means find D.
  • "Select the word-pair with the same relationship" means pick a whole pair like the given one.
  • Some questions give three pairs: A : B :: C : D :: E : ?. Use both complete pairs to confirm the rule.
  • Some give the answer side and hide the first term (? : 176 :: 14 : 126). Work the rule backwards.

concepts.title: The sentence test for word analogies
concepts.body:
Make a short, exact sentence for the given pair, then put each option into it.
  • Doctor : Hospital, "A doctor works in a hospital." Teacher : School fits. Teacher : Book does not.
  • If two options fit, make the sentence sharper: "A young cow is called a calf" is sharper than "a cow is related to a calf".
  • Keep the order the same. Hospital : Doctor is the reverse of Doctor : Hospital and is wrong.
SSC adds a note: "the words must be considered as meaningful English words and must not be related to each other based on the number of letters, consonants or vowels". So only meaning counts in these questions.

concepts.title: Number-pair rules
concepts.body:
Test these rules in order on the given pair:
RuleExample
n²7 : 49
n³4 : 64
n² ± n6 : 42 (36 + 6), 6 : 30 (36 − 6)
n³ ± n6 : 222 (216 + 6)
n² ± k or n³ ± k3 : 28 (27 + 1), 17 : 4914 (4913 + 1)
(n ± k)²4 : 49 = (4 + 3)², 6 : 81 = (6 + 3)²
n × k ± c16 : 240 = 16 × 15, 6 : 90 = 6 × 15
square root ± k961 : 992 = 961 + 31 (31² = 961)
Look at the size: if B is about n², think squares; if about n³, think cubes; if a fixed multiple, divide B by A.

concepts.title: Number sets (triads) and the whole-number rule
concepts.body:
Sets like (24, 15, 120) and (21, 19, 133) link three numbers. Try:
  • third = first × second ÷ k (24 × 15 = 360, 360 ÷ 3 = 120),
  • third = (first + second) × k, or first − second = second − third (equal steps, like 66, 57, 48),
  • middle = (first + third) ÷ 2, or middle² = first × third.
SSC adds: "operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into its constituent digits. E.g. 13: operations on 13 such as adding, subtracting or multiplying 13 can be performed. Breaking 13 into 1 and 3 is not allowed." So never use digit sums in these questions.

Always confirm the rule on both given sets before testing options.

concepts.title: Letter-cluster moves
concepts.body:
Write letter positions (A = 1 … Z = 26) above both clusters and compare letter by letter.
MoveExample
Same shift for every letterACE : BDF (+1 each)
Growing shiftPDK : QFN (+1, +2, +3)
Mixed shiftCAT : DCW (+1, +2, +3)
Opposite letters (sum 27)ABC : ZYX
Reverse orderWOLF : FLOW
Swap pairsJKLM : KJML
Shift and reverseABC : FED (each +3, then reversed)
When the answer has two blanks (# : DKR :: PCL : %), the same rule works forwards on one side and backwards on the other. Check each option in both directions.

concepts.title: Word-to-number analogies
concepts.body:
A word is turned into a number. Common ways:
  • Sum of positions: CAT = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24.
  • Sum of reverse positions (Z = 1 … A = 26): A = 26, B = 25.
  • Product of positions, or sum × number of letters.
  • Positions written side by side: BAD = 2 1 4 = 214.
  • Number of letters × something.
Find which one gives the first number exactly, then apply it to the new word.

concepts.title: Figure analogies
concepts.body: Compare figure A with figure B and name every change: rotation (by 45°, 90° or 180°, clockwise or anticlockwise), mirror flip, inside and outside shapes swapping, shading changing, a part added or removed, number of sides changing. Apply exactly the same changes to figure C. Remove options that break any one change.

concepts.title: Using the options smartly
concepts.body:
Analogy options are close to each other. Save time:
  • For number pairs, test only the fastest rule first (square, cube) on the options; one option often fits at once.
  • For letter clusters, check only the first letter of each option, then the second.
  • For word pairs, cross out options whose relationship is reversed or only loosely related.

varieties.name: Word analogy
varieties.how: Make an exact sentence for the given pair ("A is used to clean B"), keep the same order, and test each option in that sentence.

steps: Sentence: toothpaste is used to clean teeth.
A broom is used to clean the floor.

varieties.name: Letter-cluster analogy
varieties.how: Write the positions of each letter in both clusters and find the shift for each place. Apply the same shifts, place by place, to the new cluster. Also check for reversal or opposite letters.

steps: P → Q is +1, D → F is +2, K → N is +3.

varieties.name: Number-pair analogy
varieties.how: Test squares, cubes, n² ± n, n³ ± n and simple multiples on the first pair. Confirm on the second pair, then apply to the question number.

varieties.name: Number-set (triad) analogy
varieties.how: Find one rule that links the numbers inside each given set, without splitting numbers into digits. Confirm it on both sets, then test each option set.

steps: (b) gives 52, (c) gives 70, (d) gives 36. None of them fit.

varieties.name: Word-to-number analogy
varieties.how: Try the sum of letter positions first, then reverse positions, product, or positions written side by side. Use the rule that gives the first number exactly.

steps: C + A + T = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24. Rule: sum of positions.

varieties.name: Figure analogy
varieties.how: List every change from figure A to figure B (rotation, flip, inside and outside swap, shading, parts added or removed) and make the same changes to figure C.

example.q: Figure A is a small circle inside a square. Figure B is a small square inside a circle. Figure C is a small star inside a triangle. What is figure D?
steps: From A to B, the inner and outer shapes swap places.
Swap the star and the triangle in figure C.
example.answer: A small triangle inside a star.

tips: For words, make an exact sentence and keep the order of the pair the same.
For numbers, try n², n³, n² ± n and n³ ± n first. Most SSC number analogies use one of these.
If three pairs are given, use the two complete pairs to confirm the rule before checking options.
In number sets, never split a number into digits; SSC says so in the question note.
For letter clusters, compare place by place and write the shift (+1, +2, +3) above each letter.
Check the first letter or the last digit of every option first; it often removes three options at once.
traps: Reversed pairs: Hospital : Doctor is not the same as Doctor : Hospital.
A loose link is not enough. Teacher : Book is related, but Teacher : School matches "works in".
A number rule that fits the first pair may fail the second. Always check both.
Wrap-around in letter shifts: Y + 3 = B.
Some letter-analogy words are real words (WOLF : FLOW). Ignore the meaning; only the letter positions matter.

questions.q:
Select the option that is related to the third word in the same way as the second word is related to the first word.
Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
questions.solution:
A doctor works in a hospital.
A teacher works in a school.
So the answer is School.

questions.q:
Select the number that can replace the question mark (?).
4 : 16 :: 7 : ?
questions.solution:
Rule: second number = square of the first.
4² = 16.
7² = 49.

questions.q:
Select the option that is related to the third letter-cluster in the same way as the second letter-cluster is related to the first.
ACE : BDF :: GIK : ?
questions.solution:
A→B, C→D, E→F: each letter +1.
G+1 = H, I+1 = J, K+1 = L.
Answer: HJL.

questions.q:
Select the number that can replace the question mark (?).
3 : 28 :: 5 : ?
In a certain way, CAT is related to DCW. In the same way, DOG is related to:
questions.solution:
C→D (+1), A→C (+2), T→W (+3).
Apply +1, +2, +3 to DOG:
D+1 = E, O+2 = Q, G+3 = J.
Answer: EQJ.

questions.q:
Select the number that can replace the question mark (?).
6 : 222 :: 8 : ?

flashcards.back: Say the relation of the first pair in one sentence, test it, then apply it to the second pair.
